rv.q: You’ll have to book a seat at the Shubert Theatre, where the play had its official opening Wednesday night, for all the frenzied shenanigans that slake one’s thirst for sweet political revenge — a dish here served hilariously superheated.
This silly, fast-paced lark gets the spectators laughing often with a well-cast ensemble of pros.
So Fillinger, her killer cast, and director Susan Stroman go hard in scene after scene. If you laugh, they win — and they really want to win.
When a cast is having this much fun, it's impossible not to be in on it.
Fresh, funny and full of spunk, “POTUS” may in fact be saner than the truth.
As a farce, “POTUS” still plays by old and almost definitionally male rules; farce is built on tropes of domination and violence.
By the time Hough starts with the Boot Scootin’ Boogie, POTUS can lead us just about anywhere it wants to go.
Up until this point, the quippy, expletive-laced dialogue elicited laughs, but now the jokes grow redundant.
The non-stop high energy desensitizes by Act 2.
POTUS is a heck of a good time and a hell of a laugh.
Ms. Stroman, meanwhile, proves once again that her own leadership abilities should be held in no doubt.
And while such vulgarity may turn some theatergoers off, it will send many others (such as myself) into frequent fits of unbridled laughter.
This second half loses the zany drive of the first.
If there is a stand-out among these stand-outs, it is probably Julianne Hough as Dusty
Were it not for Stroman and her cast, POTUS would not work nearly as well as it does — honestly, I don't think it would work at all.
Ultimately, POTUS goes for an easy ending by teasing the audience with the possibility of a female president and female retribution.

Watching POTUS, however, I must report—many will agree with me— that the comedy is just about the funniest to split sides on Broadway this comedy-short season or, let’s be even more enthusiastic, any number of seasons past.

Here, it’s not the president but his wife (Vanessa Williams), lesbian sister (Lea DeLaria), paramour (Julianne Hough), a female reporter (Lilli Cooper) and his female staff (Rachel Dratch, Suzy Nakamura, and Julie White) who are the real incompetents.
I am elated to admit that sitting through the play and having my jaw hurt from laughing, made me eat my words before I could even say them.
Because beneath the hard, sweet shell of this comic jawbreaker is a bitter abscess filled with rage.

cn.t: This raucous feminist farce delivers frequent laughs through vulgarity and slapstick, powered by a stellar all-female cast, though critics find the chaos uneven—hilarious when firing on all cylinders but occasionally losing steam.
